lesson.title: Gatekeepers of the Membrane: The Three Major Families of Surface Receptors
lesson.summary: Cell surface receptors are membrane-embedded proteins that let a cell detect signaling molecules too large or too polar to cross the plasma membrane, and nearly all of them fall into one of three structural and mechanistic families.
lesson.body:
Many of the body's most important signaling molecules, including peptide hormones like insulin, neurotransmitters like acetylcholine, and local mediators like epinephrine, are too large, too polar, or too charged to cross the hydrophobic interior of the plasma membrane on their own. A cell that needs to detect these signals cannot simply wait for them to diffuse inside. Instead it relies on cell surface receptors: transmembrane proteins with an extracellular domain that binds the ligand, one or more membrane spanning segments that anchor the receptor in the bilayer, and an intracellular domain or associated machinery that carries the signal onward once binding occurs.

The plasma membrane's structure is what makes this arrangement work. Because the membrane is a fluid mosaic of phospholipids with embedded proteins, a receptor can sit stably within it, held in place by the hydrophobic match between its membrane spanning stretches of amino acids and the surrounding lipid tails, while still being free to change shape or move laterally within the bilayer when a ligand binds. The extracellular ligand binding domain relies on the same specific, reversible fit described for ligand-receptor binding generally, but here that binding pocket is displayed on the outside of the cell precisely so that circulating or locally released signals can reach it without needing to cross the membrane themselves.

Cell surface receptors fall into three major functional categories. G protein-coupled receptors, the largest family, are built from a single polypeptide that threads back and forth across the membrane seven times, and they work by activating an associated intracellular G protein when a ligand binds. Receptor tyrosine kinases have a single membrane spanning segment and carry catalytic enzyme activity in their own cytoplasmic tail, typically requiring two receptor molecules to come together before that activity switches on. Ligand gated ion channels are receptors that are also channels: ligand binding directly opens a pore that lets specific ions flow across the membrane, producing an extremely fast electrical response, which is how acetylcholine triggers muscle contraction at a neuromuscular junction.

Although these three families differ enormously in structure and mechanism, they share the same basic job: converting an extracellular binding event into an intracellular change without ever letting the ligand itself enter the cell. They differ mainly in speed and scope. Ion channel receptors act in milliseconds because they need no intermediate steps, just a physical pore opening. G protein-coupled receptors and receptor tyrosine kinases act more slowly, over seconds to minutes, because they must first activate a chain of intracellular relay molecules, but that extra machinery allows their signals to be amplified, integrated with other pathways, and shaped in ways a simple channel cannot achieve.

It is worth noting what cell surface receptors are not built to handle: lipid soluble signals such as steroid hormones, which can cross the plasma membrane directly and are instead detected by intracellular receptors located in the cytoplasm or nucleus, a completely different strategy covered later in this chapter. The next two sections look closely at the two enzyme linked families introduced here, G protein-coupled receptors and receptor tyrosine kinases, tracing exactly how binding on the outside of the cell gets converted into a transduced signal on the inside.
